Global existence results for the anisotropic Boussinesq system in dimension twoThanks: 1Université Paris-Est, Laboratoire d’Analyse et de Mathématiques Appliquées, UMR 8050, 61 avenue du Général de Gaulle, 94010 Créteil Cedex, France. Raphaël Danchin1 and Marius Paicu2
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study the global existence issue for the two-dimensional Boussinesq system with horizontal viscosity in only one equation. We first examine the case where the Navier-Stokes equation with no vertical viscosity is coupled with a transport equation. Second, we consider a coupling between the classical two-dimensional incompressible Euler equation and a transport-diffusion equation with diffusion in the horizontal direction only. For the both systems and for arbitrarily large data, we construct global weak solutions à la Leray. Next, we state global well-posedness results for more regular data. Our results strongly rely on the fact that the diffusion occurs in a direction perpendicular to the buoyancy force.

1. Introduction

The Boussinesq system describes the influence of the convection (or convection-diffusion) phenomenon in a viscous or inviscid fluid. It is used as a toy model for geophysical fluids whenever rotation and stratification play an important role (see for example J. Pedlosky’s book [23]). In the two-dimensional case, the Boussinesq system reads:

(Bκ,ν) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u−ν​Δ​u+∇Π=θ​e2withe2=(0,1),div​u=0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{2}\quad\hbox{with}\quad e_{2}=(0,1),\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0.\end{cases}

Above, u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) denotes the velocity vector-field and θ=θ⁡(t,x)\theta=\theta(t,x) is a scalar quantity such as the concentration of a chemical substance or the temperature variation in a gravity field, in which case θ​e2\theta\,e_{2} represents the buoyancy force. The nonnegative parameters κ\kappa and ν\nu denote respectively the molecular diffusion and the viscosity. In order to simplify the presentation, we restrict ourselves to the whole plan case (that is the space variable xx describes the whole ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}) and focus on the evolution for positive times (i.e. t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}).

In the case where both κ\kappa and ν\nu are positive, classical methods allow to establish the global existence of regular solutions (see for example [6, 18]). On the other hand, if κ=ν=0\kappa=\nu=0 then constructing global unique solutions for some nonconstant θ0\theta_{0} is a challenging open problem (even in the two-dimensional case) which has many similarities with the global existence problem for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations.

The intermediate situation where the diffusion acts only on one of the equations has been investigated in a number of recent papers. Under various regularity assumptions on the initial data, it has been shown that for arbitrarily large initial data, systems (Bκ,0)(B_{\kappa,0}) with κ>0\kappa>0 and (B0,ν)(B_{0,\nu}) with ν>0\nu>0 admit a global unique solution (see for example [1, 7, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20]).

In the present paper, we aim at making one more step toward the study of the system with κ=ν=0\kappa=\nu=0 by assuming that the diffusion or the viscosity occurs in the horizontal direction and in one of the equations only. More precisely, we want to consider the following two systems:

(1) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u−ν​∂12u+∇Π=θ​e2div​u=0\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u-\nu\partial_{1}^{2}u+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{2}\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0\end{cases}

and

(2) {∂tθ+u⋅∇θ−κ​∂12θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇Π=θ​e2div​u=0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\partial_{1}^{2}\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\Pi=\theta e_{2}\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0.\end{cases}

Let us stress that the anisotropic viscosity or diffusion assumptions are consistent with the study of geophysical fluids. It turns out that, in certain regimes and after suitable rescaling, the vertical viscosity (or diffusion) is negligible with respect to the horizontal viscosity (or diffusion) (for more details, one may refer to [11]). For the standard three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, the first mathematical results concerning anisotropic viscosity have been obtained in [10, 22].

On the one hand, it is clear that small variations over the classical methods for solving quasi-linear hyperbolic systems would give local well-posedness for Systems (1) and (2) with initial data in Sobolev spaces with suitably large index. On the other hand, since diffusion occurs in only one direction and one equation, it is not obvious that those solutions are actually global. The present paper is dedicated to the study of global existence for the initial value problem associated to Systems (1) and (2) with (possibly) large initial data.

Let us emphasize that, in contrast with the previous studies devoted to the Boussinesq system, all the results presented here strongly rely on the fact that the buoyancy force is vertical. As a matter of fact, it is not clear at all that if the direction of the force is changed then having horizontal diffusion allows to improve significantly the results compared to the case κ=ν=0.\kappa=\nu=0.

Let us now briefly explain where the direction of the buoyancy force comes into play, and give an insight of the main arguments that we used in the proofs. In the case of System (1), the vorticity ω:=∂1u2−∂2u1\omega:=\partial_{1}u^{2}-\partial_{2}u^{1} satisfies

∂tω+u⋅∇ω−ν​∂12ω=∂1θ,\partial_{t}\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega-\nu\partial_{1}^{2}\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,

from which we easily get (at least formally)

12dd​t∥ω∥L22+ν∥∂1ω∥L22=−∫ℝ2θ∂1ωdx.\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\omega\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\nu\|\partial_{1}\omega\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\theta\>\partial_{1}\omega\;dx.

Taking advantage of the Young inequality and of the fact that ‖θ⁡(t)‖L2≤‖θ0‖L2,\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}, it is thus possible to get a bound for ω\omega in Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,L2).L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}). In fact, it turns out that similar arguments enable us to bound stronger norms of the solution so that it will be possible to prove the global existence part of Theorem 1. As the velocity field that we have constructed fails to be Lipschitz, proving uniqueness requires our using losing estimates for transport or transport-diffusion equations in the spirit of [3, 12, 13, 14].

If we consider System (2) then the vorticity equation reduces to

∂tω+u⋅∇ω=∂1θ,\partial_{t}\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,

so that one may write

12​dd​t​‖ω‖L22=∫∂1θ​ω​𝑑x.\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\omega\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\int\partial_{1}\theta\>\omega\;dx.

Now, it turns out that the temperature equation in System (2) provides us with the following bound:

‖θ⁡(t)‖L22+2​κ​∫0t‖∂1θ⁡(τ)‖L2​(ℝ2)2​𝑑τ≤‖θ0‖L22.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{1}\theta(\tau)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}d\tau\leq\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Therefore, using Young’s inequality, it is still possible to get a global control on ω\omega in Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,L2).L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}). In order to get a global result with uniqueness however, we have to consider initial data with much more regularity. Indeed, we have to observe that System (2) contains the Euler system as a particular case (just take θ≡0\theta\equiv 0) so that, according to Yudovich result in [24] one can barely expect to have uniqueness if the vorticity is not in L∞.L^{\infty}. Now, from the vorticity equation, it is clear that bounding the vorticity in L∞L^{\infty} requires that ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta is in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L∞)L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}). If we assume that OPENθ0∈H1)\theta_{0}\in H^{1}) then we shall be able to prove that the horizontal smoothing effect ensures that ∇θ\nabla\theta is in Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H1).L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1}). As the space H1H^{1} fails to be embedded in L∞L^{\infty} however, we will have to assume even more regularity in the horizontal direction, and to check that this additional regularity is preserved for all positive time. These plain considerations explain the assumptions made in the statement of Theorem 2. As for uniqueness, it will follow from adaptations of the Yudovich method in [24].

The paper unfolds as follows: section 2 is devoted to the study of System (1) whereas Section 3 deals with System (2). A few technical lemmas have been postponed in the final section of the paper (in particular losing a priori estimates for transport equation with anisotropic diffusion).

As usual, we agree that CC denotes a harmless positive constant, the meaning of which is clear from the context.

2. The case of an horizontal viscosity

This part is devoted to the study of the initial value problem for System (1) under various regularity hypotheses. We aim at getting global results for possibly large data.

More precisely, in the first subsection, we prove that for any data (θ0,u0)∈L2×H1(\theta_{0},u_{0})\in L^{2}\times H^{1} with div​u0=0,\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0, System (1) admits at least one global solution with finite energy. The next subsection is devoted to a local well-posedness result for smooth data, together with a continuation criterion involving the L∞L^{\infty} norm of (θ,∇u).(\theta,\nabla u). In subsection 2.3, we state a sharper continuation criterion involving a weaker norm of the velocity which is (formally) controlled for all time by System (1). This will enable us to state that the system is globally well-posed in Sobolev spaces with large enough index (see Theorem 5). The last two subsections are devoted to the proof of our global existence and uniqueness result for rough data (namely Theorem 1).

2.1. Global weak solutions

In order to motivate our statement, let us first write out the “natural” energy estimates associated to System (1).

On the one hand, because div​u=0,\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u=0, we have

    (un2)n∈ℕ(u_{n}^{2})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded in Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H2).L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{2}).

This is enough to pass to the limit (up to extraction) in (10). Indeed, putting together the continuous embedding H1↪L4H^{1}\hookrightarrow L^{4} and Hölder inequality, we see that the first two properties imply that (θn​un)n∈ℕ(\theta_{n}u_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded in Ll​o​c4​(ℝ+,L43)L^{4}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\frac{4}{3}}) whence, by embedding, in Ll​o​c4​(ℝ+,H−12).L^{4}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{-\frac{1}{2}}). Therefore (∂tθn)n∈ℕ(\partial_{t}\theta_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded in Ll​o​c4​(ℝ+,H−32).L^{4}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{-\frac{3}{2}}). Since the embeddings H−32↪L2H^{-\frac{3}{2}}\hookrightarrow L^{2} and H−1↪H1H^{-1}\hookrightarrow H^{1} are locally compact, the classical Aubin-Lions argument (see e.g. [2]) allows to conclude that, up to extraction, sequence (θn,un)n∈ℕ(\theta_{n},u_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} has a limit (θ,u)(\theta,u) satisfying System (1) and that

θ∈L∞​(ℝ+,L2),u∈Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,H1)​ and ​u2∈Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H2).\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}),\quad u\in L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\ \hbox{ and }\ u^{2}\in L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{2}).

From standard arguments relying on the time continuity of (θ,u)(\theta,u) in low norms, it is easy to prove the weak time continuity result. Finally, since θ\theta is transported by the flow of a divergence free vector-field with coefficients in Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H1),L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1}), we get in addition that θ∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,L2)\theta\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}) (see e.g. [16]).  

2.2. Local smooth solutions

Here we aim at proving the local well-posedness for System (1) with initial data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in Hs−1×HsH^{s-1}\times H^{s} for some s>2.s>2.

The proof will follow from an energy method once the system has been localized in dyadic frequencies. This localization may be done by means of a nonhomogeneous Littlewood-Paley decomposition. In order to define the dyadic blocks Δq\Delta_{q} used in this decomposition, one may proceed as in [8]: starting from a couple (χ,φ)(\chi,\varphi) of smooth nonnegative functions such that

Suppχ⊂{ξ∈ℝ2/|ξ|≤4/3},Suppφ⊂{ξ∈ℝ2/ 3/4≤|ξ|≤8/3},\hfil\displaystyle\,\mbox{\rm Supp}\,\chi\subset\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,/\,|\xi|\leq 4/3\},\qquad\,\mbox{\rm Supp}\,\varphi\subset\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,/\,3/4\leq|\xi|\leq 8/3\},
χ⁡(ξ)+∑q≥0φ⁡(2−q​ξ)=1for all ​ξ∈ℝ2,\hfil\displaystyle\chi(\xi)+\sum_{q\geq 0}\varphi(2^{-q}\xi)=1\quad\hbox{for all }\ \xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

we set

Δq:=0 if q≤−2,Δ−1:=χ(D)andΔq:=φ(2−qD) if q≥0.\Delta_{q}:=0\ \hbox{ if }\ q\leq-2,\quad\Delta_{-1}:=\chi(D)\quad\hbox{and}\quad\Delta_{q}:=\varphi(2^{-q}D)\ \hbox{ if }\ q\geq 0.

We also introduce the low frequency cut-off

Sq:=∑p≤q−1ΔqS_{q}:=\sum_{p\leq q-1}\Delta_{q}

and (for technical purposes) the modified low frequency cut-off S¯q\overline{S}_{q} defined by

(14) S¯−1=Δ−1=S0andS¯q=Sqifq≠−1.\overline{S}_{-1}=\Delta_{-1}=S_{0}\quad\hbox{and}\quad\overline{S}_{q}=S_{q}\quad\hbox{if}\quad q\not=-1.

It may be easily checked that

u=∑q≥−1Δq​ufor all tempered distribution ​uu=\sum_{q\geq-1}\Delta_{q}u\quad\hbox{for all tempered distribution }\ u

and that the set of tempered distributions uu satisfying

(∑q≥−122​q​s​‖Δq​u‖L22)12<∞\biggl(\sum_{q\geq-1}2^{2qs}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{2}}<\infty

coincides with the Sobolev space Hs,H^{s}, the above left-hand side defining a norm equivalent to the usual one.

Let us now state the main result of this subsection:

Proposition 4.

Let (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) be in Hs−1×HsH^{s-1}\times H^{s} with s>2.s>2. Assume that div​u0=0.{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0. There exists a positive time TT depending only (continuously) on ν\nu and on ‖(θ0,ω0)‖Hs−1\|(\theta_{0},\omega_{0})\|_{H^{s-1}} such that System (1) admits a unique solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) in 𝒞⁡([0,T],Hs−1×Hs).{\mathcal{C}}([0,T];H^{s-1}\times H^{s}). Moreover, u2∈L2​([0,T],Hs+1).u^{2}\in L^{2}([0,T];H^{s+1}).

Proof:  The uniqueness is a straightforward consequence of a more general result (see Proposition 9) the proof of which is postponed to subsection 2.5. So let us focus on the existence part of the above proposition, which is mostly a consequence of the Hs−1×HsH^{s-1}\times H^{s} a priori estimates associated to System (1).

1. A priori estimates in Hs−1×HsH^{s-1}\times H^{s}

Let (θ,u)∈𝒞1​([0,T],H∞)(\theta,u)\in{\mathcal{C}}^{1}([0,T];H^{\infty}) satisfy (1). We claim that there exists a constant CC depending only on ss and such that for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], we have

In order to get a Hs−1H^{s-1} estimate for ω,\omega, one may apply Δq\Delta_{q} to the vorticity equation. With the above notation, we get

and, according to (70),

Therefore

Multiplying both sides by 22​q​(s−1)2^{2q(s-1)} then summing up over q≥−1,q\geq-1, we end up with

It is now clear that adding up this latter inequality to (16) then applying Gronwall lemma completes the proof of Inequality (15).

One can use again the Friedrichs method introduced in the proof of Theorem 3. As Operators JnJ_{n} are orthogonal projectors for all Sobolev spaces, they do not modify the energy estimates leading to Inequality (15). Therefore, the approximate solution (θn,un)(\theta_{n},u_{n}) to (10) satisfies

Therefore, there exists a c>0c>0 such that if we set

(17) T:=2​ν​log⁡(cν​‖(θ0,ω0)‖Hs−1)T:=2\nu\log\biggl(\frac{c}{\nu\|(\theta_{0},\omega_{0})\|_{H^{s-1}}}\biggr)

then

Mimicking the compactness argument used for proving Theorem 3, one can now conclude that there exists a solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) satisfying (θ,u)∈L∞​([0,T],Hs−1×Hs)(\theta,u)\in L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{s-1}\times H^{s}) and u2∈L2​([0,T],Hs+1).u^{2}\in L^{2}([0,T];H^{s+1}). The time continuity follows from the fact that θ\theta and ω\omega satisfy transport equations with Hs−1H^{s-1} initial data and a L2​([0,T],Hs−1)L^{2}([0,T];H^{s-1}) source term. 2.3. Global smooth solutions

Here we aim at proving that the local smooth solutions which have been constructed so far may be extended to all positive time. Exhibiting a polynomial control of ‖∇u​(t)‖L\|\nabla u(t)\|_{\sqrt{L}} (where the space L\sqrt{L} has been defined in (3)) is the cornerstone of this extension. More precisely, we shall first prove that the L1​([0,T],L​L)L^{1}([0,T];LL) norm of ∇u\nabla u with

(18) LL:={f∈𝒮′/∥f∥L​L:=supq≥0‖Sq​f‖L∞q+1<∞}LL:=\biggl\{f\in{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}\,/\,\|f\|_{LL}:=\sup_{q\geq 0}\frac{\|S_{q}f\|_{L^{\infty}}}{q+1}<\infty\biggr\}

controls the Sobolev regularity of the solutions to System (1). Next, we shall state that, under the hypotheses of Proposition 4, the norm of ∇u\nabla u in L2​([0,T],L)L^{2}([0,T];\sqrt{L}) (which is stronger to the L1​([0,T],L​L)L^{1}([0,T];LL) norm) may be bounded for all time by a fixed polynomial the coefficients of which depend only on low norms of the data, and on ν.\nu. Combining this with Proposition 4 will lead to the following global existence statement:

Theorem 5.

Let (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) be in Hs−1×HsH^{s-1}\times H^{s} for some s>2.s>2. Assume that div​u0=0.{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0. Then system (1) has a unique global solution (θ,u)(\theta,u) such that

(θ,u)∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,Hs−1×Hs)andu2∈Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,Hs+1).(\theta,u)\in{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{s-1}\times H^{s})\quad\hbox{and}\quad u^{2}\in L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{s+1}).

As a first step for proving Theorem 5, let us show the following lemma:

Lemma 6.

Let (θ,u)(\theta,u) be a solution to (1) in 𝒞⁡([0,T),Hs−1×Hs){\mathcal{C}}([0,T);H^{s-1}\times H^{s}) with s>2s>2. If

∫0T‖∇u​(t)‖L​L​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T}\|\nabla u(t)\|_{LL}\,dt<\infty

then (θ,u)(\theta,u) may be continued beyond TT into a smooth solution of (1).\eqref{eq:b-vitesse}.

sup0≤t<T(‖θ⁡(t)‖Hs−1+‖ω⁡(t)‖Hs−1)<∞.\sup_{0\leq t<T}\bigl(\|\theta(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}+\|\omega(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\bigr)<\infty.

∥θ(t)∥L∞=∥θ0∥L∞for allt∈[0,T).\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\quad\hbox{for all}\quad t\in[0,T).

Let (θ,u)(\theta,u) be a solution to (1) in 𝒞⁡([0,T),H2×H3).{\mathcal{C}}([0,T);H^{2}\times H^{3}). 3. The case of an horizontal diffusivity

This section is devoted to the study of System (2). In other words, in contrast with the previous section, we now assume that the velocity satisfies the incompressible Euler equation with buoyancy force whereas the temperature experiences diffusion in the horizontal variable only.

We aim at stating various global existence results for arbitrarily large data. More precisely, we first prove that any data θ0∈L2\theta_{0}\in L^{2} and u0∈H1u_{0}\in H^{1} with div​u0=0\,\mbox{\rm div}\,u_{0}=0 generates a global weak solution with finite energy. The rest of this section is mainly devoted to the proof of Theorem 2. As a first step, in subsection 3.2, we state H1H^{1} a priori estimates for the la temperature. In the next subsection, we prove a uniqueness result for a large class of solutions. As this uniqueness result requires in particular that ∇θ∈Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L∞)\nabla\theta\in L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}) and that ∇u∈Ll​o​c1​([0,T],L),\nabla u\in L^{1}_{loc}([0,T];L), our next task amounts to finding additional regularity conditions on the data which may be propagated globally by the system. It turns out that it is possible to propagate some anisotropic Sobolev regularity over the temperature, and thus to complete the proof of Theorem 2.

3.1. Global weak solutions: the case θ0∈L2\theta_{0}\in L^{2} and u0∈H1u_{0}\in H^{1}

Let us first derive the formal energy estimates for System (2) in the case θ0∈L2\theta_{0}\in L^{2} and u0∈H1.u_{0}\in H^{1}. First, multiply (2)1\eqref{eq:b-temperature}_{1} by θ\theta and integrate over [0,t]×ℝ2.[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}. We get

(35) ‖θ⁡(t)‖L22+2​κ​∫0t‖∂1θ⁡(s)‖L22​𝑑s≤‖θ0‖L22.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{1}\theta(s)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\,ds\leq\|\theta_{0}\|^{2}_{L^{2}}.

Combining this with the standard energy estimate for uu yields

(36) ‖u⁡(t)‖L2≤‖u0‖L2+t​‖θ0‖L2.\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}+t\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

In order to get a H1H^{1} bound for the velocity, one may consider the vorticity equation:

∂tω+u⋅∇ω=∂1θ.\partial_{t}\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta.

Multiplying by ω\omega then integrating with respect to the space variable, we find that

3.3. A uniqueness result

In this section, we establish a uniqueness result for System (2) under “minimal” assumptions. In order to motivate those assumptions, let us remind that in the isotropic case (that is with a full Laplacian in the temperature equation) which has been investigated in [15], uniqueness is true in the class of C0,1​(ℝ+,L2)C^{0,1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}) solutions which satisfy in addition

(41) ∇θ∈Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L∞)and∇u∈Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,L).\nabla\theta\in L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty})\quad\hbox{and}\quad\nabla u\in L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L).

As in the case that we now consider the smoothing effect over the temperature is obviously weaker, we expect the conditions leading to uniqueness to be stronger than (41). We shall prove the following result:

This paragraph is devoted to proving the following result (which obviously implies Theorem (2)):

Theorem 12.

supplemented with smoothed out initial data (θ0ε,u0ε).(\theta_{0}^{\varepsilon},u_{0}^{\varepsilon}).

Resorting again to the Friedrichs method that has been used in the case ε=0,\varepsilon=0, and noticing that the cut-off operator JnJ_{n} does not modify the Sobolev estimates, we get a global solution (θε,uε)(\theta^{\varepsilon},u^{\varepsilon}) in

𝒞⁡(ℝ+,H1)∩Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+,H2){\mathcal{C}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{2})

satisfying Inequalities (37) and (40) uniformly with respect to ε.\varepsilon.

Actually, using standard methods, one can check that the H2H^{2} regularity controls higher Sobolev norms. As the initial data are in H∞,H^{\infty}, the solution (θε,uε)(\theta^{\varepsilon},u^{\varepsilon}) thus belongs to all the Sobolev spaces, which will enable us to make the following computations rigorous.

The LpL^{p} estimate over the vorticity may be proved by multiplying the vorticity equation

∂tωε+uε⋅∇ωε−ε​Δ​ωε=∂1θε\partial_{t}\omega^{\varepsilon}+u^{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla\omega^{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon\Delta\omega^{\varepsilon}=\partial_{1}\theta^{\varepsilon}

by |ωε|p−2​ωε|\omega^{\varepsilon}|^{p-2}\omega^{\varepsilon}, and performing an integration over ℝ2.\mathbb{R}^{2}. This gives again

‖ωε​(t)‖Lp≤‖ω0‖Lp+∫0t‖∂1θε‖Lp≤‖ω0‖Lp+C​p​t​‖∂1θε‖Lt2​(H1).\|\omega^{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\omega_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{1}\theta^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\omega_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+C\sqrt{pt}\,\|\partial_{1}\theta^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}_{t}(H^{1})}.

It is also clear that all the anisotropic Sobolev estimates remain the same, uniformly with respect to ε.\varepsilon. Therefore, having ε\varepsilon tend to 00 yields the end of the existence part of Theorem 10.

Finally, the uniqueness result is a mere consequence of Proposition 11.

4.1. A few inequalities

Here we prove a few inequalities which have been used throughout the paper.

Proof of Inequality (20) : For proving (20), one may split ∇u\nabla u into low and high frequencies according to the Littlewood-Paley decomposition. More precisely, for any N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} one may write

∇u=SN∇u+∑q≥NΔq∇u.\nabla u=S_{N}\nabla u+\sum_{q\geq N}\Delta_{q}\nabla u.

∥∇u∥L∞≤∥SN∇u∥L∞+∑q≥N∥Δq∇u∥L∞,\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|S_{N}\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}+\sum_{q\geq N}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}},

whence, using the definition of ∥⋅∥L​L\|\cdot\|_{LL} and Bernstein inequalities,

∥∇u∥L∞≤(N+1)∥∇u∥L​L+C∑q≥N2q∥Δq∇u∥L2.\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq(N+1)\|\nabla u\|_{LL}+C\sum_{q\geq N}2^{q}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla u\|_{L^{2}}.

Given that ∥Δq∇u∥L2=∥Δqω∥L2\|\Delta_{q}\nabla u\|_{L^{2}}=\|\Delta_{q}\omega\|_{L^{2}} and that 2−s<0,2-s<0, we readily get

‖∇u‖L∞≤(N+1)​‖∇u‖L​L+C​2N⁡(2−s)​‖ω‖Hs−1.\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq(N+1)\|\nabla u\|_{LL}+C2^{N(2-s)}\|\omega\|_{H^{s-1}}.

Now, if C​‖ω‖Hs−1≤‖∇u‖L​LC\|\omega\|_{H^{s-1}}\leq\|\nabla u\|_{LL} then taking N=0N=0 obviously yields the desired inequality. Else, one may choose for NN the integer part of

1s−2​log2​(C​‖ω‖Hs−1‖∇v‖L​L)\frac{1}{s-2}\log_{2}\biggl(\frac{C\|\omega\|_{H^{s-1}}}{\|\nabla v\|_{LL}}\biggr)

and we still get the desired result.  

Lemma 13.

‖v‖Lp≤∑q≥−1‖Δq​v‖Lp,≤C​∑q≥−12−2​qp​ 2q​‖Δq​v‖L2,≤C​(∑q≥−12−4​qp)12​‖v‖H1,≤C​p−1​‖v‖H1,\begin{array}[]{lll}\|v\|_{L^{p}}&\leq&\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}},\\[4.30554pt] &\leq&C\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}2^{-\frac{2q}{p}}\,2^{q}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{2}},\\[4.30554pt] &\leq&C\biggl(\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}2^{-\frac{4q}{p}}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{2}}\|v\|_{H^{1}},\\[8.61108pt] &\leq&C\sqrt{p-1}\|v\|_{H^{1}},\end{array}

The second part of the appendix is mainly devoted to the proof of losing a priori estimates for the following anisotropic Stokes system with convection

(67) {∂tw+v⋅∇w−ν​∂12w+∇Π=f+g​e2,div​w=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}w+v\cdot\nabla w-\nu\partial_{1}^{2}w+\nabla\Pi=f+g\,e_{2},\\ \,\mbox{\rm div}\,w=0\end{array}\right.

Remind that those estimates are the key to the proof of uniqueness in Theorem 1. Albeit similar results have been proved before in [12], we also prove losing a priori estimates for ordinary transport equations for the reader convenience.
